message.content:
Sure! If you want to force‑close Visual Studio Code from the command line on Windows, you can use the built‑in **`taskkill`** utility.  
Here’s the simplest way:

```cmd
taskkill /IM code.exe /F
```

### What each part does

| Argument | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `/IM`    | Specifies the image name (process name) to target. In this case `code.exe`. |
| `/F`     | Forces termination – the process will be killed immediately, even if it’s hung. |

### Optional flags

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `/PID <pid>` | Target a specific process ID instead of an image name. |
| `/T` | Terminates the specified process and any child processes started by it. |
| `/FI <filter>` | Filters which processes to target (e.g., `/FI "USERNAME eq yourname"`). |

### Example: Kill all VS Code instances

```cmd
taskkill /IM code.exe /F /T
```

This kills every `code.exe` process and any children it may have spawned.

### Running from PowerShell

If you’re in PowerShell, you can also run the same command directly:

```powershell
taskkill /IM code.exe /F
```

or use PowerShell’s own cmdlet:

```powershell
Stop-Process -Name code -Force
```

### Things to keep in mind

1. **Admin rights** – If you’re trying to kill a process owned by another user or running under elevated privileges, you may need to run the command prompt or PowerShell as Administrator.
2. **Unsaved work** – `taskkill /F` will terminate the process without giving VS Code a chance to prompt you about unsaved files. Use it only when you’re sure you don’t need to preserve any state.
3. **Multiple instances** – If you have several VS Code windows open, `taskkill /IM code.exe /F` will close all of them at once.

That’s it! Just hit Enter after typing the command, and VS Code should shut down immediately.
